citation_meta.citation_title: Relational Archival Investigation: Identity, Chronology, and Historical Judgment in Korean Experimental Art

scholarly_schema.name: Relational Archival Investigation: Identity, Chronology, and Historical Judgment in Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.headline: Relational Archival Investigation: Identity, Chronology, and Historical Judgment in Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.abstract: Relational Archival Investigation (RAI) is a source-critical method for determining what relationships among records can establish about the identity, chronology, explanation and historical consequences of artworks. This study compares seven consecutive acquisition entries in the 2016 Annual Report of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), with their public collection descriptions. Two leading production-year assignments differ. Published artist testimony distinguishes production from presentation in one case, while the reason for the other difference remains open. Additional comparisons distinguish an early one-monitor presentation from a later twelve-monitor arrangement, a title’s accidental origin from its subsequent adoption, and a performance from the later repair of a photograph that records it. The study traces how accurately transcribed details can yield an unsupported historical claim when they are assigned to the same object or occasion. Post-Interpretive Criticism supplies a philosophical background. The findings rest on a bounded set of Korean experimental art cases and their documented sources.
scholarly_schema.description: A documentary study of Korean experimental art: how collection records, artist testimony and archives support claims about artwork identity, chronology, naming, performance and display. Main paper with two separately citable supplements.

scholarly_schema.headline: Documentary Evidence and Source Comparisons: Supplement 1 to Relational Archival Investigation
scholarly_schema.abstract: This documentary supplement records the sources, work identifications, comparisons and judgments supporting Relational Archival Investigation. It pairs all seven acquisition entries 73–79 on printed pages 39–40 of MMCA’s 2016 Annual Report with collection records 7922–7928 (management numbers 07909–07915) and retains agreements, discrepancies and unresolved cases. Additional sections document the Jeok–Eungnyeok inquiry, the evidence for the extended case studies and Lee Kang-so’s Paris sequence. Selected excerpts, paraphrases and institutional identifiers make the comparisons traceable. The seven-entry block was selected retrospectively. The supplement attributes descriptions and transcriptions to the institutions that published them and gives the consultation date separately from the dates of the historical events.

scholarly_schema.name: Extended Case Studies and Methodological Demonstrations: Supplement 2 to Relational Archival Investigation
scholarly_schema.headline: Extended Case Studies and Methodological Demonstrations: Supplement 2 to Relational Archival Investigation
scholarly_schema.abstract: Four cases show how Relational Archival Investigation distinguishes artwork identity from the histories of naming, documentation and display. Kim Yong-Ik’s Flat Object materials distinguish the reported origin of a title variant from its later adoption. Rim Dong Sik’s Tying Reeds and Beard photograph records an action and bears evidence of the artist’s later repair. Sung Neung Kyung’s Reading Newspaper places photographic presentation within the work’s early public history. Kim Youngjin’s 1978–2 distinguishes a one-monitor presentation from a twelve-monitor arrangement at the 2016 Busan Biennale. The supplement attributes the institutional descriptions and retrospective testimony it uses and identifies the evidence needed to pursue unresolved questions. The cases are selected demonstrations developed within the same research programme.
scholarly_schema.description: Four studies of Kim Yong-Ik, Rim Dong Sik, Sung Neung Kyung and Kim Youngjin distinguish the work from the histories of its title, photographs, performance and display.

scholarly_schema.name: When Interpretation Becomes Authority
scholarly_schema.headline: When Interpretation Becomes Authority
scholarly_schema.alternativeHeadline: Alexander V. Markov × Dorian Vale — A research dialogue between Post-Interpretive Criticism and the Semiotics of Non-intentional Ephemerality
scholarly_schema.description: Dorian Vale’s editorial account of scholarly correspondence with Alexander V. Markov. Research dialogue, version 1.0, October 2026 edition; public repository release 11 November 2026.
scholarly_schema.abstract: This research dialogue is Dorian Vale’s editorial account of written correspondence with Alexander V. Markov in September and October 2026. It examines how interpretations acquire authority through their reuse in catalogues, labels, archives, teaching, and institutional procedures. Bringing Post-Interpretive Criticism into exchange with the Semiotics of Non-intentional Ephemerality, the discussion distinguishes the preservation of a text from its continuing jurisdiction, verification from warrant migration and reauthorization, and an effective correction from the maintenance of its effects. Markov’s semantic protocol and hypothetical history of correction and lapse are considered alongside Vale’s proposals concerning contestability, distributed responsibility, and the continuity of justificatory burden. The accompanying study, After the Interpretation Changes, supplies a separately authored documentary case concerning Simon Maris’s Isabella; its evidence limits the stronger theoretical claims. The dialogue asks how time, place, and role affect the authority of records, and what would distinguish a changed answer from a change in the conditions governing it. The exchanges are condensed thematic paraphrases. Selection, framing, and wording are Vale’s responsibility; this is neither a transcript nor a jointly authored statement. Disagreement and proposals not accepted by both correspondents remain explicit.

citation_meta.citation_title: When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art

scholarly_schema.name: When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.headline: When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.description: Korean art history working paper on photography, archives and reperformance in Rim Dong Sik, Kim Kulim and Sung Neung Kyung, with sources and limits.
scholarly_schema.abstract: Photographs give Korean experimental art continuing public forms through copying, repair, printing, exhibition and collection. This article compares three documentary histories. Seoul Museum of Art describes Rim Dong Sik’s interventions in photographic records. The National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, holds a print made in 2000 of Kim Kulim’s 1970 From Phenomenon to Traces and documents a reperformance in 2016, later represented by a video in an international exhibition checklist. Sung Neung Kyung’s Reading Newspaper circulated photographically in 1976, while the present twelve-print object entered the museum’s collection in 2017. In the Korean Senior Artist Digital Archive, the researchers’ account of Sung distinguishes artworks from other performance records through exhibition, publication and artist selection. Read alongside Korean conservation scholarship, these records show how artistic recognition can be documented without establishing unchanged material survival. The comparison separates material continuity, exhibition history and institutional identification, and asks what evidence each relation requires. Collection transfer dates, classification rules and loan descriptions clarify the public histories of the objects. The dates of individual repairs, print manufacture and mounting remain bounded questions, rather than assumed links in an uninterrupted provenance.

scholarly_schema.headline: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.name: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.alternativeHeadline: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
scholarly_schema.abstract: A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable.
scholarly_schema.description: Four case studies in Korean art history trace how titles, dates and later reconstructions shape artwork identity in the records for Kim Yong-Ik, Park Suk-won, Lee Kang-so and Kim Kulim.

citation_meta.citation_title: After the Interpretation Changes: Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles

scholarly_schema.name: After the Interpretation Changes: Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles
scholarly_schema.headline: After the Interpretation Changes: Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles
scholarly_schema.abstract: This study distinguishes two changes in the Rijksmuseum’s presentation of Simon Maris’s portrait now titled Isabella: the withdrawal of a racialized catalogue title in 2015, and the fulfilment in 2020 of an announced intention to adopt a name when one became known. The second change does not, by itself, demonstrate revision of the rule governing the first. The records examined at Europeana and Wikimedia Commons reveal different afterlives of the later decision. Europeana retains the descriptive title and an account in which identification remains unfinished. Commons preserves the older wording in the name of its image file while identifying the work as Isabella in the accompanying description. Drawing on my correspondence with Alexander V. Markov, the study follows what these descriptions do, rather than treating their survival as evidence of continuing authority. It finds uneven presentation of the later naming decision, not a demonstrated restoration of the rejected title. Its contribution to Post-Interpretive Criticism is a documentary distinction among correction, completion and circulation.

citation_meta.citation_title: Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art

scholarly_schema.name: Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art
scholarly_schema.headline: Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art
scholarly_schema.abstract:
This working paper develops a claim-specific criterion of historical answerability through engagement with Reiko Tomii’s scholarship on operation in postwar Japanese art. It asks when evidence concerning exhibition, documentation, and artistic organization requires an art-historical account to reconsider the boundary of the work it claims to explain.

The principal case is Shiraga Kazuo’s Challenging Mud. Tomii’s accounts of material preparation and anticipated display are read beside Namiko Kunimoto’s analysis of action, object, agency, and selfhood. Further investigations address press presentation and photographic selection, Hi Red Center and GUN, conditions of authorization, and the differentiation of events and photographic records in museum cataloguing. The comparison does not presume a disagreement between Tomii and Kunimoto or equate evidence of preparation with complete predetermination.

The method distinguishes attribution, justification, and historical accuracy. Before evaluating a challenge, it fixes a proposition’s referent, meaning, scope, certainty, and evidential basis. Retention, limitation, revision, and suspension identify possible consequences of evidence without becoming compulsory stages or an aesthetic scoring system. The analysis separates a supported preparation-display relation from stronger claims about intention and distinguishes documentation’s original public operation from the reach of its later historical testimony.

The contribution is a disciplined account of inferential reach within the historical problems Tomii’s research makes visible. It also refines the application of restraint in Post-Interpretive Criticism: the amount of explanation cannot be prescribed before its evidential function is examined. This is a source-critical study of published arguments, not an independently inspected archival reconstruction or an empirical study of museum audiences. The criterion remains open to further cases and scholarly revision.
scholarly_schema.description: Independent study of postwar Japanese art, exhibition and photographic documentation, developed following discussion and feedback from art historian Reiko Tomii. Sole author: Dorian Vale.
